text: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the list has a cycle in it. Can you solve it using constant memory?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a cycle means some node's next points back at a node I've already passed, so walking forward never ends. The shape is like the letter rho: a straight run, then a loop. And I only have to answer yes or no — you don't want the node where the loop starts?
Just yes or no. Finding the entry is a different problem.
Good. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can the list be empty, or a single node pointing at itself?
Empty is allowed, and yes, a single node can point to itself. Values can repeat.

Values can repeat — I'll come back to that, it rules something out. On the example, three, two, zero, minus four, with the last node pointing back to index one, walking from the head repeats two, zero, minus four forever, so the answer is yes. For one, two, three ending in null, I reach the end, so no. What makes this awkward is that I can't detect forever by walking — that's the whole problem. I need something that terminates either way.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would keep a hash set of node addresses as I walk. If I ever see one twice, there's a cycle; if I reach null, there isn't. That's linear time and correct, but it's linear space, which is exactly what you asked me to avoid. Walking a fixed number of steps doesn't hold up either: I don't know n, and borrowing the stated maximum would smuggle a constraint into the algorithm. This problem reminds me of Floyd's cycle detection — two pointers at different speeds. Picture a running track: if the path is a loop, the faster runner laps the slower one and they land on the same spot. If the path has an end, the faster runner hits it first. Two pointers, no container, constant space.

Here's the plan. One: slow and fast both start at the head. Two: each round, slow moves one step, fast moves two, then I compare. Three: if they meet, return true; if fast reaches null, return false. The key is the gap: once slow is in the loop, the speed difference is exactly one, so the gap shrinks by one per round and has to hit zero. One thing worth flagging: I compare pointers, not values — values can repeat, so comparing values would report cycles that aren't there. Also, both start at the head, so comparing before moving returns true for everything. I'll use a do-while so the first thing is a move; the cost is that the body runs once unconditionally, so I need a guard for empty and single-node lists. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up: a guard, then the do-while from the plan. Two details in the loop condition. Fast being null means those two steps landed exactly past the end; fast's next being null means two more steps would run off. Drop either check and the next round dereferences null — and the order relies on and short-circuiting. And the guard isn't a nicety: removing it under the sanitizers, both the empty list and a single node crash with a null-pointer access. Worth knowing: a plain while loop with the same condition checks first, so the body is always safe and the guard isn't needed at all. Both are correct; the while version fails more gently if you forget a line.

Let's dry-run the code on three, two, zero, minus four, tail back to index one; expected true. The row that matters is round two: fast goes two, three, then follows the back edge to one. Once inside the loop it can never leave, and slow walks in behind it. One round later they meet at index three — not the entry at index one, which is fine for a boolean. Without a cycle, like one through five, fast's next goes null after two rounds: false. Corner cases: empty or a single node is false, through the guard. A node pointing at itself is true in one round. One, two with the tail back to the head is true. The shape depends only on length and back-edge index, so I ran all eighteen ninety-one shapes up to sixty under the sanitizers: zero wrong.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear. Without a cycle, fast covers two nodes a round, so about n over two rounds. With one, slow needs mu rounds to enter the loop and at most lambda more to be caught, and mu plus lambda is at most n. Measured up to three hundred nodes: worst case a hundred fifty rounds without a cycle, three hundred with one. Space is constant, two pointers, read-only. Oh, one more thing — the usual reason for step two is that a bigger step could jump over. I checked: with step three, detection still works on all twenty thousand one hundred cycle shapes, because the starting gap is even whenever the loop length is even. What breaks is the entry-finding follow-up, wrong on about three in ten shapes. So use two is right, but the usual reason isn't.

Very good. Three things stood out. You explained correctness through the gap shrinking by exactly one, which is the actual reason it can't overshoot, not just the fast one catches up. You picked up on values can repeat when I said it and used it to rule out comparing values. And you checked the step-size folklore with a measurement rather than repeating it. Knowing why two is the right choice is more useful than knowing that it is.
